pipelay-installation-support.lead: We supported pipeline installation and surveyed the Tolmount gas export and methanol pipelines for Saipem.
story: From June to August 2020, Saipem contracted us for installation vessel support and survey on the Tolmount 20-inch gas export pipeline and 3-inch methanol pipeline. The pipelines run from the onshore terminal at Easington out to the Tolmount Main Platform.

Topaz Tiamat acted as support vessel for the pipelay vessel Castoro Sei. Our scope covered mattress installation, touchdown monitoring, boulder relocation, and multibeam pre-lay, as-laid, as-trenched and as-backfilled surveys.
The campaign went well and safely, with good data, low downtime, no injuries and no HSEQ incidents, and a very pleased client.

structure-inspection.lead: An IMR campaign on multiple assets off Trinidad, delivered safely, on time and within budget as the pandemic began.
story: In February and March 2020, Havila Subsea completed an inspection, maintenance and repair campaign on multiple assets on Trinidad’s north and east coast, despite the onset of the global COVID-19 pandemic.

haven-jack-up-removal.lead: We provided vessels, ROVs, survey and construction services for the removal of the Haven jack-up accommodation rig from Johan Sverdrup.
story: In April 2020, our vessels Olympic Challenger and Topaz Tiamat worked as ROV support and construction vessels during the removal of the Haven jack-up accommodation rig from the Equinor-operated Johan Sverdrup field.

Two pump skids were mobilised on each vessel and used to control the lowering of the rig towards the waterline. We were responsible for vessel, ROV, survey and construction services, and the project was completed with the highest possible client satisfaction score.

boulder-removal.lead: Boulder removal on the Troll B field, 350 m down.
story: During the summer season we cleared unexploded ordnance (UXO) with good results. Dredging at 350 m water depth on the Troll B field was a major part of the project.

suction-anchor-installation.lead: Havila Subsea and Topaz Tiamat installed 14 suction anchors in the North Sea and Norwegian Sea.
story: Havila Subsea and Topaz Tiamat installed 14 suction anchors in the North Sea and Norwegian Sea, in sizes from 5 to 18 tonnes.
Our engineering department also carried out analyses that ensured increased environmental limits as well as safe operations.

gwatch-equinor-gas-fields.lead: We are carrying out gravity and seafloor deformation surveys at several Equinor-operated gas fields in the North Sea, Norwegian Sea and Barents Sea.
story: The scope is monitor surveys at the Troll field (Troll East and Troll West), Aasta Hansteen, Snøhvit (including the Snøhvit CO2 injection site), Albatross and Askeladd, plus installation of 35 concrete pads on the Irpa field and 12 on Askeladd. Equinor awarded the work as a call-off from the multi-scope agreement.

The data will improve Equinor’s understanding of these fields and help optimise production strategies. gWatch measures gravitational variations, which give insight into the strata beneath the seabed and the characteristics of the reservoir. It uses compact instrumentation and efficient data collection, and limits harm to marine life.

Viking Reach, our newly acquired ROV survey and light construction vessel, carries the survey spread: one survey ROV, one work-class ROV and hull-mounted survey equipment. Mobilisation started on Monday 31 July.
The compact, cost-efficient equipment also shows the potential for similar surveys from Reach Remote, our remote survey vessel platform.

depthwatch-shell-4d-seismic.lead: We have used DepthWatch in ten ocean bottom node surveys for Shell in the Gulf of Mexico, cutting node depth errors from metres to centimetres.
story: 4D seismic gives time-lapse images of the subsurface that help find untapped reserves and refine extraction. Adding our DepthWatch service improves the imaging at minimal extra cost, and also maps the seabed deformation caused by hydrocarbon depletion, which helps keep installations safe.

In ocean bottom node (OBN) surveys, nodes with seismic sensors are placed temporarily on the seafloor. Precise node depths are critical: errors blur the seismic image and make changes in the reservoir harder to detect. We have deployed DepthWatch in ten OBN surveys in Shell-operated fields in the Gulf of Mexico, reducing the margin of error from metres to centimetres.

Accurate relative node depths and subsidence measurements give better OBN statics solutions, data repeatability and 4D signals. The seabed subsidence maps also help update and calibrate geomechanical and reservoir models and support field integrity. Shell presented the results at the IMAGE 2023 conference in Houston, and our Monitoring division presented them at the Second EAGE Seabed Seismic Workshop in Milan.

DepthWatch builds on gWatch, our 4D gravity and subsidence technology, which is used in all major gas and condensate fields in Norway and measures seabed subsidence to better than 2 mm over several years. DepthWatch instruments are fitted to the ROV that deploys or retrieves the nodes, so the survey takes no longer and costs little extra. One or two of our engineers run the data acquisition from the OBN vessel and from land, and the node depths are ready when seismic processing starts.
Our aim is for DepthWatch to become a standard addition to every 4D operation that deploys seabed seismic nodes from ROVs.

ormen-lange-gravimetry.lead: In the 2020 gWatch survey at Ormen Lange we cut measurement time per station by 15% and delivered the lowest station uncertainties on the field to date.
story: Shell Norge acquires gravimetry and seabed subsidence measurements at Ormen Lange every second year to monitor aquifer influx, reservoir compaction and the energy balance within the reservoir. It uses them to refine its field recovery strategy and make gas production more sustainable.

During a survey, our gWatch instrumentation measures gravity and subsidence at predefined stations on the seafloor. We repeat the measurements at each station to reach higher accuracy, so the time per station and the number of repeats drive the overall survey time.

In the 2020 survey we reduced the measurement time per station by 15% and the overall number of measurements by 13%. We also delivered the lowest total station uncertainties to date on the field: 0.61 μGal for gravity and 3.7 mm for seabed depth. This lets Shell Norge refine its estimates of reservoir properties and improve reservoir management.
gWatch surveys complement or replace 4D seismic at a tenth of the price and a third of the delivery time, so clients can survey less often or drop 4D seismic altogether.

asumo.lead: From 2018 to 2022 we adapted our seafloor deformation and gravity technology to monitor tectonically active areas, such as the subduction zone off Japan.
story: In this project (2018 to 2022) we adapt our technologies for high-accuracy vertical seafloor deformation (VSD) and time-lapse gravity measurements at the seabed to the surveillance of tectonically active areas, such as the subduction zone along the coast of Japan.
The largest earthquakes on Earth occur in subduction zones, among them Japan in 2011 (Mw 9.0) and Sumatra in 2004 (Mw 9.1). Both caused many casualties through ground shaking and tsunamis.

Plate deformation happens before, during and after such events, and it determines what types of earthquakes and tsunamis occur, where and how often. Offshore, these plate movements are only sparsely monitored, which leaves several unknowns in the model predictions. We aim to introduce seafloor 4D gravity and VSD monitoring as new sources of information that can help improve earthquake and tsunami risk mitigation.

site-survey-campaign.lead: We carried out site surveys across the Barents Sea, Norwegian Sea and North Sea in water depths of 100 to 390 m.
story: In summer 2019 our Survey division was contracted to perform site surveys using high-resolution multichannel seismic and a variety of geophysical and geotechnical sensors, and to run ROV transects for a habitat assessment. Water depths ranged from 100 to 390 m.

The scope covered a multibeam echo sounder, sidescan sonar, a sub-bottom profiler, 2D and ultra-high-resolution multichannel seismic, cone penetration testing and ROV video for environmental assessment. The charterer fitted the combined fishing and research vessel MV Christina E with the survey spread, and chartered the PSV Siem Pride for the ROV work. Christina E has a deep draft of 8 m and can fill large tanks to stay stable in adverse weather, and her drop keel carried a multibeam system able to acquire accurate bathymetry to about 500 m water depth.

The campaign was spread over locations in the Barents Sea, the Norwegian Sea and the North Sea. The survey was needed to reduce the risk of drilling through geohazards such as shallow gas and seabed obstructions, to plan the mooring spread for a semi-submersible rig at the proposed well location, and to keep the environmental impact low.

We evaluated seabed and sub-seabed conditions from all the geophysical, geotechnical and environmental data, together with the client’s 3D seismic data and background information. The deliverables were field operation, environmental (including habitat assessment), geotechnical, seismic processing and geophysical interpretation reports, a GIS database, data coverage and interpretation charts, and processed data.

pipeline-inspection-campaign.lead: We supplied the Siem Pride with survey spread and ROV for the annual inspection of Shell’s 120 km Ormen Lange gas export pipeline.
story: In summer 2020, with IKM Subsea and the vessel charterer, we were contracted by Norske Shell to provide the Siem Pride, fully equipped with survey spread and ROV, for the annual pipeline inspection of the Ormen Lange 120 km gas export pipeline. The survey also covered umbilicals and spool pieces between Nyhamna, Norway and the Ormen Lange field, in water depths of 25 to 950 m.

As survey subcontractor on board, we mobilised the vessel and a compact ROV, acquired, processed, evented and reported the data, and made the final deliveries to Shell Norway and DNV GL. The work focused on high-quality multibeam and video data to assess the integrity of the pipelines and spools.

The work is done from a relatively small vessel with low carbon emissions. It is a proven, cost-effective solution, and the same scope has been carried out for several clients over the past five years.

The final delivery to Shell includes navigation model projects and video deliverables with all events, a digital terrain model at 10 cm resolution, three-channel HD video, processed inspection deliverables for all assets surveyed and one inspection report per asset.
Our annual pipeline inspection record runs from 2016 (185 km for Shell) to 2020 (165 km for Shell), with 395 km in 2017, 133 km in 2018 and 416 km in 2019 for Shell, OKEA and Neptune Energy.

geophysical-and-uxo-power-cable-route-su.lead: As main contractor to Nexans, we surveyed three planned power cable routes to the Seagreen offshore wind farm for geophysical conditions and unexploded ordnance.
story: As main contractor to Nexans, we had full responsibility for planning and performing the work: preparation, mobilising the Siem Pride and an ROV, and data acquisition, processing, interpretation and reporting. The survey system included surface and subsea positioning, precision inertial positioning, dual-head multibeam, 600 kHz sidescan sonar, a sub-bottom profiler, a transverse gradiometer system and HD video inspection.

The operation had two parts. The geophysical survey covered a 20 m corridor with multibeam, sidescan and sub-bottom data along the centre line of the three planned routes, from the onshore transition station at Carnoustie out to the offshore platform at the Seagreen wind farm, a distance of 58 km. The UXO survey acquired gradiometer data and video along the same centre lines, with two additional winglines to get the coverage required.

The main purpose was to document the planned routes so that Nexans Norway could carry out further assessment and engineering. We established seabed conditions and potential obstructions, defined the sub-seabed soils, conditions and environmental interests, identified magnetic anomalies and potential UXO targets, and inspected the routes visually.

The final delivery to Nexans included a multibeam echo sounder digital terrain model, a sidescan sonar mosaic, a geophysical interpretation report, alignment charts, a GIS database and a field report.

digimon.lead: We contribute 4D gravity, seafloor deformation and passive seismic monitoring to DIGIMON, a project to speed up carbon capture and storage.
story: The aim of DIGIMON is to speed up the implementation of carbon capture and storage (CCS) by developing and demonstrating an affordable, flexible, societally embedded and smart digital monitoring early-warning system, for monitoring any CO2 storage reservoir and subsurface barrier system.
We contribute expertise in our core geophysical monitoring techniques (4D gravity, seafloor deformation and passive seismic monitoring) and lead one of the work packages in the project.

decomissioning-3.lead: Olympic Challenger removed several risers from an FPSO in the North Sea and prepared the site for future decommissioning.
story: In November, Olympic Challenger took part in a larger decommissioning project for a major oil and gas company on the Norwegian shelf in the North Sea. The scope included removing several risers (umbilical and flowlines) from an FPSO, and preparatory work (cleaning and inspection) for planning future decommissioning at the same location.

The products were recovered to deck through the moonpool using the 250 t vessel crane. The load was then picked up and transferred to a tensioner on deck and cut into smaller pieces with a hydraulic shear cutter. Water depth in the area is about 125 m.

sabella-sas-2.lead: We installed a 1 MW tidal turbine off Ushant Island in France for Sabella SAS, using Olympic Challenger.
story: In October, Olympic Challenger was contracted to Sabella SAS to install a horizontal axis tidal turbine 2 km south-east off the coast of Ushant Island, France. The turbine has a rated capacity of 1 MW. Its nacelle is moored to the seabed with a gravity base structure, and power is brought ashore through a jumper cable.

The vessel crane deployed the turbine and the work-class ROVs on board guided it into position. The ROVs also performed the pre- and post-installation surveys, the preparatory work and the electrical hook-up.
The turbine weighs 107 t dry, so a complex lift like this needs a capable subsea construction vessel.

diver-less-riser-flange-replacement.lead: We replaced a riser flange without divers for a Caribbean client, using two ROV systems in parallel from Havila Subsea.
story: We completed a diver-less riser flange replacement for a Caribbean client in December 2019. The work was done with two work-class ROV systems working in parallel on board Havila Subsea.
The project finished 40% ahead of schedule. Strong safety participation among the crew on board led to zero incidents during the offshore work.

autonomous-survey.lead: We introduced uncrewed surface vessel survey services in the Caribbean and completed nearshore geophysical surveys off Trinidad and Tobago.
story: We introduced uncrewed surface vessel (USV) services in the Caribbean, expanding our IMR services in Trinidad and Tobago. We also complete geophysical and geotechnical surveys for multiple clients in the region.

With joint venture partner MMT, we completed multiple nearshore geophysical surveys using an uncrewed surface vessel. USVs reduce risk by putting fewer people offshore, make operations more efficient and bring ultra-low emissions.

thruster-changeout.lead: A thruster changeout on the Balder FPSO in the North Sea.
story: Olympic Challenger successfully recovered the old 65 t thruster and then installed the new thruster on the Balder FPSO in the North Sea.

water-pipeline.lead: We helped Kalyon Insaat inspect and repair the fresh water pipeline from mainland Turkey to Northern Cyprus, including replacing a 500 m section.
story: Kalyon Insaat contracted us to assist with the inspection and repair of the pipeline that supplies fresh water from the Turkish mainland to the Turkish Republic of Northern Cyprus. The project involved complex marine operations and multiple vessels, with Olympic Challenger as one of the lead vessels.

The work included repairing and replacing a 500 m long pipeline segment, along with inspection tasks. It was completed successfully, with excellent performance from our team and the Olympic team on board.

fiber-optic-cable-installation.lead: We provided Olympic Challenger, ROV and construction services for Equinor’s installation of a 39.2 km fibre optic cable from Halten Link to Njord A.
story: In May 2020, Olympic Challenger was the platform for Equinor’s installation of a 39.2 km fibre optic cable between Halten Link and Njord A. Global Maritime led the project execution on behalf of Equinor, and we provided the vessel, ROV services and construction services.

A reel drive system with tensioners and accessories was mobilised in Kristiansund on 9 May. Preparatory subsea work was carried out until 12 May, when a suitable weather window was in place. Laying began on 17 May and was completed on 22 May.

efficient-light-construction.lead: In the first quarter of 2020 the Topaz Tiamat spread carried out light construction and survey projects for Equinor, completed with very high efficiency.
story: During 1Q 2020, the Topaz Tiamat spread was employed on various light construction and survey projects for Equinor. Highly effective subsea tools, combined with the workability of the vessel, let us complete the work very efficiently.
It was also the first project after a new battery pack was installed for hybrid propulsion. This worked well and gave about 11% fuel savings on an already fuel-efficient vessel.

black-sea-map-project.lead: We provided marine survey capability aboard Havila Subsea for the final cruise of Black Sea MAP, a maritime archaeology project.
story: Black Sea MAP is one of the largest maritime archaeological projects ever staged. Since 2015 it has investigated how the ancient environment of the Black Sea region changed, including the effect of sea-level change during the last glacial cycle.

The third and final cruise set sail from Burgas, Bulgaria on 25 August 2017 aboard R/V Havila Subsea, with MMT and Reach providing specialist marine survey capability. It ran for 25 days at sea. The team is led by the University of Southampton, with partners in Bulgaria and other countries, and used a specialist remote deep-water camera system able to supply ultra-high-definition imagery from more than 2 km depth.

The cruise was to complete the project’s data acquisition and let the team draw together conclusions from earlier findings. A group of young people from an education programme promoting STEM subjects and careers also joined the science team and the crew, and the expedition was filmed for a documentary.
